title: What space syntax is
text:
Space syntax began with Bill Hillier and Julienne Hanson at University College London. Their book The Social Logic of Space (1984) argued that the arrangement of spaces carries social meaning and can be measured. Applied to a city, the method asks two questions about every street: how easy it is to reach from everywhere else, and how often it lies on the way between other places.
It looks at the shape of the network and nothing else. I find that limit useful, because it lets me ask how much of Griffintown’s movement the layout alone can explain.

title: What space syntax is
text:
Segments and depth
The unit is the segment, a piece of street between two junctions, as in S1 Streets. Depth is the distance between two segments, counted in angles: a right angle costs 1 and a 45° turn costs 0.5 (Turner 2007, p. 542). Hillier and Iida (2005) found that counting turns matched observed movement better than counting metres. Turner also showed that ordinary street centrelines can be analysed this way, so I can use the city’s own street file.

title: What space syntax is
text:
Integration and choice
Integration measures how close a segment is, on average, to every other segment: a street with high integration is easy to get to. Network science calls this closeness centrality (Sabidussi 1966).
Choice imagines the shortest route between every pair of segments and counts how many of those routes pass through each one: a street with high choice is often passed through. Network science calls this betweenness centrality (Freeman 1977).
The results also report normalised versions (Hillier, Yang & Turner 2012, pp. 160, 165 and 191). NAIN rescales integration so that networks of different sizes can be compared. NACH does the same for choice and evens out its skew, where a few streets score very high and most score low. The paper gives two versions of NAIN, so I compare numbers only within one (Reading closely).

title: What space syntax is
text:
Natural movement
Hillier, Penn, Hanson, Grajewski and Xu (1993) called their central claim “natural movement”: the shape of the network is a main driver of how many people walk each street. The full references are in Resources.






NoteStill debated



The claim is influential, and its strength varies with place and land use. In the 1993 paper itself, the correlation between integration and movement across ten parts of King’s Cross ranged from 0.25 to 0.80, and shops could multiply movement beyond what the layout predicts (Hillier et al. 1993, pp. 31, 46). Ratti (2004, p. 492) adds that results depend on how the map is drawn and that the method leaves land use out. So in Situ the claim is something I test in Griffintown.

title: What space syntax is
text:
Radius
The analysis can be limited to a distance around each segment, called the radius. At 400 m it asks how central a street is within about five minutes’ walk; radius n has no limit, which here means the whole island. Studies usually take 400 to 800 m as the low radius and 4,000 to 8,000 m as the high one (van Nes & Yamu 2021, p. 65). My analysis uses 200, 400 and 800 m and radius n for walking, and 1200 and 2000 m for driving. A street can be central at 400 m and peripheral at radius n, and that contrast often tells me more than any single value.

title: What space syntax is
text:
A made-up town
I invented this town so the numbers can be checked by hand, with depth counted as one step per change of street. It has a main street (M1 to M5), cross streets to the north and south, a back street (B1, B2) and a cul-de-sac (C1, C2).



Depth from M1, then integration, then choice, on the same made-up town.



DepthIntegrationChoice


Starting from M1 at depth 0, every street one step away has depth 1, the next ones depth 2, and so on. C2, at the end of the cul-de-sac, is six steps away.


M3 has the highest integration (0.55), because it sits in the middle. C2 has the lowest (0.24), because every other street is far from it.


M4 has the highest choice (55), because routes from the west side to the east side and to the cul-de-sac must cross it. C1 has 15, since every route to C2 passes through it. A dead end like C2 scores 0.









TipWhat the toy shows



M3 is the best place to be, and M4 is the best place to pass through. The two measures differ, so I keep both.

title: What space syntax is
text:
Why I use it

A measuring stick
My agents never read space syntax values. I compare their movement with the values afterwards, so the comparison is a real test. Agents that preferred high-scoring streets would make it circular: the answer would go in and come back out.
Choice is already a route model built on the least-turning route between every pair of segments (Turner 2007, p. 544). Walkers who took those routes, spread evenly over all pairs, would match choice by construction, and the match would prove nothing. So the walkers in S7 pick routes for their own reasons, such as where they are going and the time of day. Space syntax enters Situ only at the end, in S9 Observer.


What the comparison can show

Where the walkers and choice agree, the layout alone may explain the movement. Where they disagree, something else is at work, such as a building or a rule.


The city’s movement counts check the model against reality, and they are thin: seven S1 junctions, one to three days each, between February 2024 and May 2026. Enough to raise a warning, too little to prove anything.


In the game I can watch whether players drift toward integrated streets, which bears on my research question about wayfinding.





Why this method
It runs in QGIS on the city’s open street file, and the same file with the same settings gives the same values. Forty years of studies use it, so I can set Griffintown beside other cities. It was built to study how layout and social life relate, the subject of my research. Its blind spots are well documented, and each one falls to another Situ system.


What this means for my data
Values belong to the network they were calculated on. A missing path makes its neighbours look less connected than they are, so I added the city’s off-street paths before the analysis (The walking network).
The edge of the map also distorts: streets near it look peripheral only because the map stops there (Ratti 2004, p. 496; van Nes & Yamu 2021, p. 51). So the analysis covers the whole island, and I cut Griffintown out of the results afterwards.

title: S6 Streetscape
text:
S6 says what stands on Griffintown’s streets besides the buildings: trees, fire hydrants, benches and other furniture, street lights, surveillance cameras, pedestrian crossings, the sidewalks and traffic islands themselves, and the road works under way on the day I saved the city’s list. Each object keeps its source, its values as the source gives them, and the S1 street it stands on.
S6 decides nothing about what these objects do. A tree may shade a walker or hide a shop; a hydrant forbids a car to stop beside it. Those effects belong to the systems after S6, S7 Walkers and S8 Drivers, where each effect will be written down as an assumption. What a walker can see from where they stand will be part of S7, built from the S4 buildings and these trees.

title: S6 Streetscape
text:
What it found

971 trees · 104 hydrants · 806 street lights · 487 sidewalk pieces · 29 road works




What stands on the streets. White circles: older or undated trees; grey: trees planted since 2013, each sized by its trunk. Pink: hydrants and road works.


The streetscape is young (certain, for what the city records). Of the 775 public trees with a planting date, 651 were planted in 2013 or later, and three quarters of all trunks measure less than 18 cm across. Of the 267 sidewalk pieces with a construction date, 175 were built in 2020 or later. The commonest species are elms, honey-locusts, poplars and Kentucky coffeetrees.
My reading, and it is an interpretation: Griffintown’s street furniture is as new as its towers, and its trees are still small. A view along a street today is probably more open than it will be in twenty years, so any study of what can be seen here describes a moment in a growing place.
The 286 pieces of furniture, from benches and bicycle racks to drinking fountains, all come from OpenStreetMap, since the city’s furniture file covers only its large parks. Mappers may have missed some (likely). The city lists 29 road works in the area on 16 October 2026, from sidewalk rebuilding on Saint-Martin to construction work on Young that runs until June 2027.

title: S6 Streetscape
text:
Read by a machine

Street lights
The city publishes no file of its street lights (certain, for its open data catalogue). OpenStreetMap records 72 in the area. Mapillary, where people and the city upload street photos, runs software over every photo that detects objects, street lights among them, and places each one on the map. It found street lights in 888 places here. Detections less than 3 m apart are joined into one light, since a pole often carries two heads, which leaves 764. Counting a light found by either source once, the area has 806.



Street lights. White: found in photos by Mapillary’s software; grey: the same, found in no photo since 2023. Pink rings: lamps in OpenStreetMap.


How far can a machine’s reading be trusted? The hydrants offer a test, since the city’s file lists every one. Of the 82 hydrants Mapillary’s software found, 68 stand within 5 m of one of the city’s, half of them less than a metre away, and it found 68 of the city’s 104. Where its photos reach, it is mostly right and well placed, and it misses about a third (likely; some misses may be streets no photo covers).
The two sources of lights barely meet. Only 30 of OpenStreetMap’s 72 lamps have a detection within 5 m, and most of the others line the east end of Rue des Bassins and Allée des Barges, where the sheet shows almost no detections at all. Those are walking streets beside the basins, and most photos are taken from cars (likely). The machine sees what the camera passed, and a walker’s street may be the one it knows least.


Crossings and cameras
The same software finds surveillance cameras and the paint of pedestrian crossings, and OpenStreetMap records both. The two readers agree on crossings and barely on cameras.



Cameras and crossings. Filled marks: found in photos by Mapillary’s software, fainter when no photo since 2023 shows them. Rings: the same kinds in OpenStreetMap.


Crossings are where the machine and the mappers meet. Of the 102 painted crossings Mapillary’s software found, 74 stand within 5 m of a crossing OpenStreetMap records as painted or signalled, half of them less than 2 m away. OpenStreetMap records 481 crossings, 289 of them unmarked, and the photos find 83 of its 192 painted ones. Six painted crossings in the photos stand where OpenStreetMap says there is no paint: a crossing painted since, or a tag nobody updated (guessing).
The cameras barely overlap: 34 from the photos, 55 in OpenStreetMap, 2 in both. Most of OpenStreetMap’s cameras are tagged as private outdoor cameras along Wellington, Young and Murray, probably mapped by someone reading building fronts (likely), and a few are the city’s traffic cameras at corners of Peel and de la Montagne. The software’s cameras spread across the area, six of them on Rue William. Each reader finds a different set of watchers, and neither finds them all.
The software also finds poles, and S6 leaves them out. The street lights already say which streets are lit, and the number of poles depends mostly on how close two detections must be to count as one.


Benches, bins and racks
For benches, bins and bicycle racks, the machine and the mappers agree too little for either to fill the other’s gaps. Mapillary’s software finds 320 bins where OpenStreetMap has 38, and many are probably household bins set out on collection day (guessing). S6 keeps those detections out of its objects and reports the comparison in its tests.

title: S6 Streetscape
text:
What S6 leaves out
The city’s tree inventory covers public trees only, so trees in courtyards and on private land are missing. The city’s canopy model and aerial LiDAR date from 2015, before most of today’s towers and trees, so S6 does not use them. The city’s art data holds a single subsidized mural in the area and none of its own public art collection; the artworks OpenStreetMap records are already among the S4 places. The city publishes no file of its street lights, so S6 takes them from OpenStreetMap and from photos.

title: S6 Streetscape
text:
Checkpoints
Five road works are still listed although their permits ended the day before I saved the file (K01 to K05). They may have been extended, or the list may lag behind the street. Thirty-five objects were found only in photos taken before 2023 (K06 to K40): 26 street lights, 6 painted crossings and 3 cameras. Griffintown has been rebuilt street by street since then, and some may be gone.

title: S5 Rhythm
text:
S5 gives each hour of the week what the open data says about it. Henri Lefebvre proposed reading a city through its rhythms, the repetitions of days and seasons (Lefebvre 2004). S5 is the first system in Situ that holds time, and it starts from two kinds of evidence that I keep apart.
The first is measured: how busy the streets are, hour by hour, from the city’s movement counts at S1 junctions. The second is promised: which places say they are open, from the opening hours S4 gathered. A count records what happened on one day. An opening hour records an intention, and a place can be open and empty. S5 never mixes the two, and a later system that reads S5 knows which one it is reading.
Neither one is a simulation. S5 offers S7 and S8 a clock to time their walkers and drivers by, and it offers S9 a measured day to compare them with.

title: S5 Rhythm
text:
What was measured

9 counted days · 7 junctions · no weekend

The city counted seven S1 junctions on nine days, all of them midweek, from Tuesday to Thursday. Only J040, where Guy meets Ottawa and William, was counted around the clock, for three days in December 2024. The other six were counted on a single day, in three windows that cover the two rush hours and midday.
Junctions differ in size: J051 on Notre-Dame sees about four times the people J006 on Ann sees. So S5 compares shapes. Each day is divided by its own average over the six hours every day counted (7h, 8h, 11h, 12h, 16h and 17h), which makes 1.0 an ordinary daytime hour of that day. A weekday hour then takes the mean of the days that counted it, with their lowest and highest. How S5 is built gives the rules.



A weekday, hour by hour. White: the mean of the counted days. Grey band: lowest to highest. Pink: hours counted at J040 alone.


The shape has a value for every hour of a weekday, and 17 of the 24 hours rest on J040’s three December days alone (certain). Everything from 18:00 to 6:00 is one junction in winter.
My first reading, and it is an interpretation: people on foot have a sharper evening than morning, peaking at 17h at about one and a half times an ordinary hour, against just over one at 8h. Bicycles peak twice, at 8h and 17h. Cars spread their busy hours from 16h to 19h. On Wellington, on the one Thursday in February when four of its junctions were counted, Murray and Young carried the most vehicles at 8h, and Ann and Shannon at 17h. Only one day stands behind that difference, so it stays a question for the field.

title: S5 Rhythm
section: Bicycles, every day of the year
text:
Bicycles, every day of the year

376 days · 3 detectors · 59 Saturdays, 57 Sundays

The city also keeps permanent bicycle detectors, which record every hour of every day. Three stand inside the study area: two on Peel at Ottawa, one for each direction, and one on William at Nazareth, westbound. All three were complete on 376 days between 9 June 2025 and 14 October 2026. For bicycles, S5 can therefore speak about weekends and seasons. Each day is read the same way as the counts, against its own reference hours.



Bicycles all year. Above, the day’s shape by kind of day and season. Below, the bicycles of an average day, month by month.


The year has a strong swing (certain, for these three detectors). An average day in August or September brings about 1,800 to 1,900 bicycles past them, against 130 to 180 from December to February, roughly ten times fewer. The week matters less: in summer a Saturday brings nine tenths of a weekday’s bicycles, and a Sunday about three quarters.
The kind of day changes the shape more than the amount. Every weekday, in every season, has two sharp peaks, at 8h and 17h. Saturdays and Sundays have no morning peak at all: bicycles build through the day to a long afternoon, highest between 13h and 17h. My reading, and it is an interpretation: on weekdays these streets carry a commute, and on weekends an outing.
The two sources agree where they meet. On weekdays the counts’ bicycle shape follows the detectors’ closely, with a correlation of 0.89 over the 24 hours (likely a real agreement, since the streets and the years differ). The largest gap is at 19h in winter, where the counts rest on J040 alone. Two more detectors stand on Peel at Notre-Dame, just outside the area, and S5 leaves them out.

title: S5 Rhythm
text:
What the places promise

83 of 558 places give their hours

Of the 558 places S4 found, 83 give opening hours (15 %), almost all through OpenStreetMap. Restaurants and cafés lead; the rest are mostly shops, bars, banks and parks. The other 475 stay unknown at every hour. S5 never reads a missing hour as closed.



Places open each hour of the week, among the 83 that give hours. A place counts as open in an hour when it is open at half past.


The promised week peaks around midday from Tuesday to Friday, with 73 places open at its height, and thins on Sunday to about 56. By 21h fewer than 30 remain. Two places give hours S5 cannot read with certainty, and they are its checkpoints: Henden opens at 19:00 with no closing time (H01), and SHAY’s brunch rule, read the way the tag’s grammar says, replaces its weekend dinner hours (H02).

title: S5 Rhythm
text:
What S5 cannot say yet
The bicycles now have weekends and seasons; people on foot and cars still have neither. The places say Saturday is almost as open as a weekday, and no count of walkers exists to tell whether they come. The counts fall in February, May, November and December, while the bicycles show how much summer changes a street. The three detectors stand on two streets, so they tell the rhythm of cycling on Peel and William, which may differ from the canal path’s. Lingering escapes every count, since a count records people passing a point and says nothing of those who stay.
The rhythm diaries and rhythm maps of my fieldwork will add a third kind of evidence, people’s own account of their week, once ethics approval comes (Limits of the desk).

title: S5 Rhythm
text:
In the Lab
In the Lab, the S5 tab sets a day and an hour. Places light up when they say they are open, and each counted junction grows with that hour’s count. Play the day to watch it fill and empty. On a Saturday or a Sunday the junctions stay empty rings, since nothing was counted. Switch to bicycles and choose a season, and the three detectors grow with the hour on any day of the week.

title: S4 Buildings
text:
S4 says what each building in the study area is: what it is used for, how tall it is, how many people live in it, and what is on its ground floor. S1 to S3 say where people can move, and nothing about why they would go anywhere. A street is busy at noon because of what lines it: a bank, a café, a gym, five hundred condos. S5 Rhythm reads S4 to know which places open when, and S7 will read it for where trips start and end.
Most answers come from the city’s tax roll, the official list of every property and what it is. When the roll is silent, I fall back on OpenStreetMap, the open map anyone can edit, and the ground floor comes from the city’s 2025 survey of street-level commercial spaces. Each answer keeps its source, and a value no file knows stays empty, with the reason. One value is an assumption: no open file says where the doors are, so I link each building to the nearest walkable street. How S4 is built gives every source and rule.

title: S4 Buildings
text:
One building, step by step
District Griffin sur Peel is the long low block on Rue Peel between Ottawa and William, with towers on top. OpenStreetMap draws it as one outline tagged retail. The tax roll places 496 properties on its lot: 494 condo dwellings, a shopping centre and a condo parking space. The roll speaks first, so S4 calls the building residential and keeps the retail tag on record, unused.
The 2025 survey finds ten premises on the ground floor, among them three banks and two restaurants; one space is vacant. Seven of the shops also appear in OpenStreetMap under the same name, and S4 counts each once. The nearest walkable street is Rue Ottawa, 6.5 m away.
The block shows the main weakness of S4. Counted by property, the condos outvote the shops 494 to 1, yet on the street the block reads as a shopping strip. So S4 keeps the ground floor apart from the use: “used for” says what most of the building is, and “ground floor” what a walker passes.

title: S4 Buildings
text:
What it found
There are 296 buildings in the study area. The tax roll gave the use of 188 and OpenStreetMap of 74. The other 34 stay unknown, mostly small sheds and annexes. Most buildings with a known use are residential, and together they hold 11,954 dwellings, a total the stress tests show to be steadier than any single tower’s count.
In the Lab, the S4 tab colours the buildings by use or by source. Click one to see each value with its source, along with the places inside it and its street.

UseSource





What each building is used for. Pink dashed outline: no source says. Pink X: B01, 415 properties at one address with no outline.







Where each building’s use came from. White: the tax roll. Grey: OpenStreetMap. Pink dashed: nowhere, so it stays unknown.

title: S4 Buildings
section: What I still need to check
text:
What I still need to check
S4 flags 61 cases for me to look at by hand, also listed in the Lab. Most are buildings whose use no source gives. Some are ties between two uses. A few stand far from any walkable street, Hangar 1825 most of all. In ten, the lot and the address point name different buildings; the largest, Griffix, is why S4 now reads the lot first.
The case that matters most is 1485 rue des Bassins (B01): 415 properties built in 2024, 290 dwellings and 125 condo parking spaces, all at one address point with no building on it. I first took it for a building OpenStreetMap had not drawn yet. The lot outlines changed my reading. The lot of 1485 holds Bass 4 and Le Vittorio, 130 m from the address point, and neither tower has a single property placed in it. So the dwellings most likely belong to those two towers, and the address point is what is out of place (likely). No file says which tower holds how many. Until a door number or a site visit settles it, I leave them unplaced, outside the 11,954 dwellings, and split nothing by guess.

title: S3 Rules
text:
S3 gives the S1 streets their traffic rules. Picture a driver arriving at a junction. S3 answers four questions for them: must I stop here, are there traffic lights, where may I go next, and how fast may I drive. It reads three of the city’s files, and every rule points back to the sign or city record it came from.
The city lists lights and speed limits directly. Stops and turns are harder. The sign file says where each sign stands and what it says, never which street it faces, and a corner sign often stands close to two or three streets at once. S3 works out the street from where the sign stands and what it would mean there (how S3 is built), and street photos settle the few places I could not decide from the desk (S3 checks with photos).

title: S3 Rules
text:
One junction, step by step
Junction J027 is where Rue Chatham ends at Rue William, in the west of Griffintown.



Rue Chatham is one-way towards William and must stop. Its two turn signs allow only the left.



Three street ends touch J027: Rue Chatham, and Rue William on each side of it. A car can arrive along each, so S3 makes three approaches. An approach is one street, driven towards the corner.
A stop sign stands 10 m before the junction and 5 m to the right of Chatham, where a stop sign for Chatham would stand. It fits no other street, so Chatham must stop.
Two more posts carry “left turn only” signs, both on the right of Chatham, 4 to 8 m before the junction.
From Chatham a car can turn onto William to the left or to the right. S3 names each move by how much the car’s heading changes: about 90° to the left is a left.
The signs allow only the left, so the right is forbidden, with the reason written beside it.
One end of William has its own stop sign and the other has none. So at J027 some streets stop, and there are no lights.

In the Lab, click any junction, then a street arriving at it, to see each rule with the sign behind it.

title: S3 Rules
text:
What changed in October
S1 gained its edge this month. I also rewrote how a sign finds its street, because I suspected my own matching caused the turn conflicts and no-entry disagreements. The new rules are mostly common sense about how signs are put up: a sign belongs only to a street it actually stands on, and panels on one post face the same drivers unless they contradict each other. Turn signs that fit only one street more than doubled, and the places to check fell from 83 to 27.
Mapillary’s street photos then settled the last turn contradiction, at Wellington and Ann (J006), and every no-entry disagreement, bringing the places to check down to 21.

Places still to check
Seven of the 21 are Autoroute 10 and its ramps, which the city’s speed file does not cover. Six are signs I could not give to any street, and three are signs the photos could not settle (decisions P03 and P06) (still open). title: S3 Rules
text:
What S3 does not know
The city’s file says where the lights are and nothing about their timing. Movement counts and light timing estimates it where the city counted traffic, and elsewhere the cycle will be a procedural assumption in S8. Some turn rules hold only at certain hours, and S3 keeps them on at all hours until S5 Rhythm gives the simulation a clock.
An exit is where an edge street meets the rest of the city, and S3 cannot see the streets beyond it. A junction there may look like an all-way stop when a street beyond does not stop, and the junction’s note says so.

title: How S3 is built and tested
text:
Approaches
A sign speaks to drivers arriving from one direction, so S3 starts from the approaches: each segment end, as a car drives towards the junction. For each one it records the arriving car’s heading, whether the one-way rules let a car arrive or leave along it, the segment’s length, and whether the junction is an exit, where the edge street meets the rest of the city. A one-way street pointing away from a junction gets no rules there, since no car arrives that way.
crumbs: How S3 is built and tested

title: How S3 is built and tested
section: How a stop sign finds its street
text:
How a stop sign finds its street



A made-up junction. Left: where a stop sign must stand to belong to a street. Right: how a turn gets its name. To try it on real junctions, open the Lab.


In Québec a stop sign usually stands on the right of the street, just before the junction, and S3 relies on that. A post fits an approach when it stands up to 35 m before the junction and 1 to 20 m to the right of the centre line, on that same segment: a post further back belongs to the previous junction, which matters on short pieces like the 20 m stretches where Wellington splits in two. When several approaches fit, the one closest to the usual spot (about 7 m to the right, near the junction) wins, and S3 marks the link as less sure. On a one-way street signs often stand on both sides, so a post on the left is accepted too. A sign that fits nothing goes on the list to check.
crumbs: How S3 is built and tested

title: How S3 is built and tested
section: How a turn sign finds its street
text:
How a turn sign finds its street
Turn signs often stand across the junction or on a median, so their position is a weak clue. S3 adds a second one: what the sign would mean on each nearby street. At J027, “left turn only” on Rue Chatham keeps the left onto William and removes the right. On Rue William a car can only go straight on, since Chatham is one-way towards William, so the same sign would remove the only move and trap every car. The signs therefore belong to Chatham.
A turn sign thus belongs to a street only when it keeps at least one of its moves and removes at least one. When several streets pass, the post decides first: panels on one post usually face the same drivers, so a turn sign that means something on the street of a stop sign on the same post goes there. Position decides next, with a sign before the junction, on the right, preferred, and one past the junction used only when nothing before it fits.
Two contradicting panels on one post, like “straight only” above “left or right only”, stand back to back, so the second one looks for another street. If none fits, it goes on the list, since only a photo can tell which way each faces. A turn sign at an exit is ignored, because the streets it points to lie outside the network. If the turn signs on one street together leave no move at all, S3 sets them aside and keeps every move open; after the photo checks, no street is in that state.
My first version placed turn signs by position alone, like stop signs, and left many streets with no way out (X5 repeats it).
To name a turn, S3 compares the arriving heading with the direction of the street the car leaves along. Less than 30° either way counts as straight on, and anything sharper is a left or a right (Chatham onto William turns 89° to the left). S3 never makes a U-turn.

text:
Decisions from photos
For the few signs I could not place from the desk, I wrote down what Mapillary’s street-level photos show (S3 checks with photos). S3 reads those decisions before its own matching, so a photo outranks a guess. The city’s file is never edited, so removing a decision brings back S3’s own matching.

title: How S3 is built and tested
text:
No-entry signs
S1 already takes its one-way streets from the city, so S3 uses no-entry signs only to check S1. A sign agrees when a street near it is one-way towards the junction, or closed to cars. When only a path I added in S1 explains it, it goes on the list, because my own decision cannot confirm itself.

title: How S3 is built and tested
text:
Traffic lights
The city’s light file gives each light a point and the names of the streets it stands between. S3 gives each light to the closest junction within 25 m. A light 25 to 100 m from every junction goes on the list, since it may mark a junction S1 is missing. The names give a second check: “Montagne / Wellington” should stand where Rue de la Montagne meets Rue Wellington.

title: How S3 is built and tested
text:
Speed limits
The city’s speed file uses the same street ids as S1, so most segments simply take their own limit. Seven segments have a limit of 0, and all seven are closed to cars, so S3 reads 0 as “no limit given”. Three Wellington pieces were redrawn after the file was made and have new ids. For those, S3 takes the speed of same-name lines lying along the segment within 5 m, when they cover nearly all of it and agree. I chose 5 m by looking at those three segments, as the smallest distance that covers the two short pieces where Wellington splits; a stress test shows what other distances give.

title: How S3 is built and tested
text:
Tests

Ten checks
Each check asks one plain question of the rules S3 writes. Eight must pass, and all eight do; the other two only report. The Lab shows the latest results.




Question
Answer




T1
Does every street a car can arrive along have exactly one approach?
yes


T2
Does every sign get a street, or a written reason it has none?
yes


T3
Does every stop sign stand where a driver would see it?
yes


T4
Do the turns fit the street layout, with a reason for every forbidden turn and no street left a trap?
yes


T5
Does each junction’s control agree with its approaches?
yes


T6
Do the no-entry signs agree with the city’s one-way streets?
report: none of the 78 disagrees, and 67 agree


T7
Does every rule cite the signs behind it?
yes


T8
How sure is each link between a sign and a street?
report: see S3 Rules


T9
Does every light stand within 25 m of its junction and name at least one of its streets?
yes


T10
Does every speed match the city file, with a reason for every gap?
yes



A disagreement in T6 goes on the list of places to check, because I cannot tell from the desk which source is right. The photos explained the last four.






TipTesting the tests



A test that always passes proves nothing. Before trusting T9 and T10, I moved one light by 30 m and changed two speed cells, one from 30 to 50 and one empty cell to 0. T9 caught the light and T10 caught both speeds. Then I put the files back.




Stress tests
Each stress test changes one thing on purpose and counts how many rules move. Run twice on the same input (X1), S3 gives identical results.
X2 moves every sign post at random, by up to 1, 2, 4 and 8 m. Up to 2 m almost nothing changes. Beyond that, ten streets change their stop at 4 m, and 28 at 8 m. So the city’s sign positions would have to be off by more than 2 m to shift the stop rules. I do not know yet how accurate they are, and a few corners are worth checking on the ground.



X2: the further every post moves, the more rules change.


X3 and X4 change how far before the junction, and how far to the right, a sign may stand. Both sit on a plateau: a little more or less than my 35 m and 20 m changes nothing, and only the tightest values lose signs. Most signs without a street stand at exits or beyond the edge.
X5 places turn signs by position alone, as my first version did, and leaves 25 streets with no turn at all. With the meaning test and the photo decisions, none is left that way.
X6 changes how close a light must be to its junction. From 25 to 40 m the same 31 junctions get lights. At 5 m eight are lost, mostly on Robert-Bourassa and on edge streets, where the city places the light 5 to 10 m away on a wide corner. At 80 m, lights start landing on the wrong junctions.
X7 changes how far a same-name line may lie when a street is missing from the speed file, and it is the one setting with no plateau below it. Under 5 m, two Wellington pieces open to cars lose their limit; from 5 m on, all three redrawn pieces are covered, which is what I chose 5 m for (speed limits). Autoroute 10 and its ramps are never in the file, at any distance.

The rules I assumed decide who may walk or drive where. I check the result twice: against itself in the tests, and against the street, with photos, in Checks and decisions.

title: S1 Streets
text:
Words



A made-up street that shows every word S1 uses.


A segment is a piece of street between two junctions, and a junction is where segment ends meet. Griffintown stays part of the city, so S1 also keeps the streets just outside the boundary that touch the study area. I call them the edge. A gate is where the study area meets the edge, and an exit is the far end of an edge street, where the city carries on. A dead end is a junction with only one segment that is neither a gate nor an exit. A one-way arrow shows the only direction cars may use; pedestrians may always walk both ways. A checkpoint, with an id starting with C, is a place where I doubted the data and took a decision from photos.
S1 starts from the city’s street lines, the same lines my space syntax analysis uses. Space syntax is the method Bill Hillier and Julienne Hanson began for describing where each street sits in the whole network; S2 attaches its values to S1. Every segment keeps the city’s own id, so any value can be traced back to its source.

title: S1 Streets
text:
Result

232 segments inside · 32 on the edge

Before the checks, S1 had 190 segments and 12 dead ends. Now it has 2 dead ends. A road map is a poor walking map: the city’s file left out the canal path and the new park paths, and 10 of the 12 dead ends turned out to be places where walkers continue.

What changed in October
The October rebuild came from decisions about the boundary and a few street ends. Every segment and junction that existed before kept its number.
The boundary is a drawing decision. The city codes Boulevard Robert-Bourassa as a pair of one-way roads about 60 m apart, and the boundary ran between them, so inside the study area the boulevard carried traffic one way only. S1 now takes in both carriageways (C19) and keeps the edge around the whole area.
At the street ends, the Lachine Canal path (C16) and two park paths (C18) came in for walkers. A footway now runs from the end of Brennan through the block to de la Commune (C04, C12), and the end of Ann joins it (C05). These links are assumed, and drawn in pink until a photo or a visit confirms them. From the end of Smith, a 41 m link crosses the plaza of Place des Aiguilleurs (C06); that one was settled with photos.

Names and rulesEvery id





Sheet A.







Sheet B: look up any S or J id in the tables.





The sheets are turned so the street grid sits level. The data itself is never turned, and the N arrow points to true north.

title: S1 Streets
text:
From here to there
In the Lab, choose S1, then “from here to there”, and click a start and an end junction. Everything it shows comes from the network alone:







Measure
What it tells you




Shortest route
the shortest way along the streets, on foot or by car; the other measures are compared with it


Directness
route length divided by the straight line; a grid gives about 1.3, and a barrier such as the canal pushes it higher


Variety
in pink, every street a trip at most 0, 5, 10, 25 or 50 % longer than the shortest could use; a thin band means the layout funnels everyone onto one street


Cost of one-way streets
how much longer the drive is than the walk between the same two junctions



From William at Young to further along William is 306 m on foot and 966 m by car, because William is one-way and the car has to go round the block. From Bassins at Rioux to Notre-Dame at Robert-Bourassa, a 10 % detour opens up 82 other segments, the grid giving walkers many ways. From Bassins at Allée des Barges to Wellington, the walk is 1.7 times the straight line, because the canal has few crossings.
These measures say nothing about how anyone actually chooses a route: people do not all take the shortest way, and the turn bans and stops of S3 are left out. Routes also stay inside the study area, so many trips by car need the city outside, and the Lab says so when that happens. How people choose belongs to S7 Walkers and S8 Drivers, whose routes will be measured against this yardstick. The Lab notes describe how the measures themselves are tested.

title: How S1 is built and tested
text:
The edge
People and cars come and go across the boundary, so S1 keeps the edge and treats it by the same rules as the inside, for walkers and for the direction of cars. The tests, and later the agents, treat the rest of the city as reachable from the exits. S3 reads the signs on the edge too, so a junction on the boundary sees every street that meets it. Later systems decide what to do with the edge: S4 puts no buildings there, and S9 measures inside the boundary only.

Numbering

title: How S1 is built and tested
text:
Joining an added path
Each end of an added path joins whatever is nearest within 25 m: a junction, or a street that gets cut at that spot. A junction wins when it is at most 5 m further away. A street dead end within 25 m of the middle of a path is joined to it too, which is how the Allées reach the canal. A decision taken from a photo may instead name the street to join, and reach up to 60 m.

title: How S1 is built and tested
text:
Two ideas behind it

Inside or outside?How far can I get?


To decide whether a point lies inside the study area, imagine a line going right from it and count how many times it crosses the outline. An odd count means inside. The method is called ray casting, and S1 applies it to the halfway point of each segment.


Start at one junction and take every allowed move, then every move from each place you reached, and so on. The method is called breadth-first search, and each round is one step. The reach view in the Lab plays it round by round.

Reach, in the Lab

title: Reading closely
text: Many sentences on this site lean on a book or a paper. In October I went back to each of those texts with the page open, to see whether my sentence still said what the author said. Most did. A few had drifted, usually by a small step, and the drift was always in the same direction: towards what my model needed the reading to say. Those few cases taught me the most.

title: Reading closely
text:
Where my sentences had drifted
I had written that people “tend to keep going roughly straight”, citing Hillier and Iida. Their claim is narrower. People judge routes by how much they turn (Hillier & Iida 2005, p. 476), which is a statement about how routes are compared, and says little about what a walker does at each corner. The difference will matter when S7 gives walkers a way to choose their routes.
I had also written that 2000 m is a common radius for driving. Hillier, Yang and Turner call radius 2000 “safe to use” for cities in general (2012, p. 165). They say nothing about cars. Using it for driving is my choice, and the S2 page now says so.
A third sentence claimed that walkers who always take the route with the least turning would reproduce the choice values (how often a street lies on the way between other places) by construction. That holds only if trips are spread evenly over every pair of places (Turner 2007, p. 544). Real trips are not, since people go to work and to shops far more often than to a random corner. I added the condition.
The last case is about my own reading. The definition of a spatial culture I use, “a distinctive way of ordering space”, comes from Hillier (1989), but I know it only through Griffiths and von Lünen’s quotation of it (2016, p. xxiii). I have kept it, and I say plainly that it is second-hand.

title: Reading closely
section: What held, and what it leaves open
text:
What held, and what it leaves open
The claim the whole method rests on did hold. Hillier and his colleagues found that the layout of the street network is “the main generator of patterns of movement” (1993, p. 29). The same paper also shows how much that depends on place: across ten parts of King’s Cross, the correlation between layout and counted movement ranges from 0.25 to 0.80 (p. 46), and shops can multiply movement beyond what the layout predicts (p. 31). Ratti (2004) adds that the results shift with how the map is drawn. Together they are my reason for keeping space syntax out of the simulation and using it only as a measuring stick.

title: Reading closely
section: Checking the software against the papers
text:
Checking the software against the papers
PlanX, the QGIS plugin I use for the analysis, follows the published measures. Two details matter before comparing its numbers with other studies.

Does PlanX count a journey once, or once each way?
PlanX’s manual leaves this open, and its own output answers it. Take a street segment that leads into a dead end and meets only two other lines at its far end. Every journey from the dead end passes through it, and no other journey does, so its choice value is simply the number of those journeys. In 103 such cases, PlanX’s value is the number counted once per pair of places, never the doubled one. So PlanX counts each pair once, as Turner defines choice (2007, p. 544). Another tool that counted both ways would give somewhat higher normalised choice values (likely), which matters before comparing Griffintown with a published study.


Which NAIN?
For normalised choice (NACH), PlanX reproduces the published formula exactly. For normalised integration (NAIN), the paper gives one form in its text and another in its appendix, and PlanX uses a third.

As a last check, Hillier, Yang and Turner (2012, p. 162) report that real cities have a mean NACH between about 0.7 and 1.2. Montréal on my walking network has 0.80, which suggests the network was built and analysed in an ordinary way.

title: Reading closely
text:
Still to read
Decoding the City by Offenhuber and Ratti (2014) will matter once the project turns to images and video of the street. The Depthmap handbook and manual will matter when I compare PlanX with Depthmap. Where this site cites Lefebvre’s Rhythmanalysis and the archival readings, the pages are given beside each quotation.
Close reading tells me whether a sentence matches its source. Whether the source is right is a separate question: several of these readings are still debated, and I try to say so where I use them.

title: Limits of the desk
text:
Where the files fall short
The first limit is purpose. No file describes a city in general. Each was made by an institution to do a job, and its categories serve that job. Scholars of data make the same point: data are gathered and shaped for a purpose before anyone analyses them (Gitelman 2013; Kitchin 2014). When I borrow a file for a different question, its categories come with it.
The city’s street file is a road file. It left out the canal path and the new park paths, and 10 of the first 12 dead ends in S1 turned out to be places where walkers carry on. The tax roll is a file for taxing property. It counts a condo parking space as a property, as it counts a home, and gives a tower’s storeys only for some kinds of property.
The second is time. Every file has its own date, and Griffintown changes faster than most of them. The city’s sign post at one corner under the Wellington viaduct is from October 2025, while every photo of it is older (P03). The city’s 3D model of 2020 stops at the Ville-Marie borough line, so Griffintown, in Le Sud-Ouest, has only the model of 2016, older than many of its towers. When two files disagree, the cause is often a gap in time.
The third is coverage. The speed file has no limits for Autoroute 10 and its ramps. The traffic light file says where the lights are and nothing about their timing. No open file says where the doors of buildings are. OpenStreetMap is drawn by volunteers, so a building appears only once someone draws it.
The fourth is position. A point in a file stands in for a thing on the street, and the two are rarely in the same spot: an address point often stands at the curb, a shop’s point on its façade. At 1485 rue des Bassins, 290 dwellings share one address point 130 m from the two towers on their lot (B01). Even my own arithmetic can move things: an early version of S4 placed some building centres tens of metres off, because of the way it handled large map coordinates.

title: Limits of the desk
text:
Seeing from the desk
Photos and videos let me look at the street without being there, and they settled real questions, among them most of the no-entry disagreements in S3. Mapillary photos from 2016 and 2024 showed that walkers cross Place des Aiguilleurs at the end of Rue Smith (C06). A walking video filmed on 11 July 2026 shows the signs at the entrance of Allée des Vraquiers: a pedestrian zone, closed to bicycles and to every vehicle except emergency ones.
Still, a camera goes where its owner walks, and it records one moment. Neither of the two recent walking videos reaches the end of Rue Brennan, so the footway I assumed there (C04) is still unconfirmed. A sign seen edge-on hides which street it faces, and a photo older than the sign it shows can mislead.
So every decision keeps its source and its date, and I grade the evidence. A link I assume is drawn in pink. A photo or a video can make it likely, and only a visit makes it confirmed. Videos are cited by link and timestamp, and no frame appears on this site unless its owner agrees.

title: Limits of the desk
text:
People are missing
The deepest limit is about people. Open data records a city’s infrastructure. Apart from the city’s movement counts at a few intersections (Movement counts), it says almost nothing about how people use the streets: where they linger, or when a corner fills. Situ aims to mediate and archive Griffintown’s spatial culture, which Hillier described as a distinctive way of ordering space (About), and its urban rhythm. Both live in what people do. From the desk I can describe the stage. I cannot yet describe the play.

title: Limits of the desk
text:
Carrying the gaps
A value no source gives stays empty, with the reason written beside it, never a zero or a guess. Every assumption is labelled as one on the page and in the Lab, and every place the desk could not settle becomes a checkpoint with a question.
So Situ describes Griffintown as its files and other people’s cameras record it, at dates I can name. It shows how the layout and the rules shape the movement that is possible; how people actually live in the area is still beyond it. Each system says which of the two it is doing.
Most remaining checkpoints can only be closed on site. The next step is a walk through Griffintown with these questions in hand, photographing and dating each answer. Later, observation of people in place will add to S5 Rhythm, the first system about time, which so far knows only weekdays.

title: Lab notes
text:
The Lab is one map with a tab for each system, where I try a system and see the places it still leaves open. Clicking anything shows what every system knows about it.
The Lab replays results and never recomputes them. Every street colour and slider position shows something a system already wrote down; the reach slider, for instance, steps through how far S1 found you can get from a junction. Each rule therefore lives in one place, and the Lab cannot quietly disagree with it.
Routes are the one small exception. Storing every route between every pair of junctions would take many megabytes, so I store only the shortest distances and the last step of each shortest route. title: Movement counts and light timing
section: Estimating the lights with Webster’s method
text:
Estimating the lights with Webster’s method
S3 knows where the 31 lights in S1 are, but the city does not publish its timing plans, so the timing is my estimate.
Webster’s method (Webster 1958) is the classic way to set a fixed light cycle from counted traffic: it asks how full each approach is, and which cycle length keeps the delay smallest. I apply it to the busiest counted hour. An approach’s load is the cars arriving per hour (a bus or truck counts as two) divided by what its lanes, taken from OpenStreetMap, can pass while green, about 1,800 cars an hour per lane. Each phase takes its fullest approach, and the phases add up to a total load. Webster’s formula turns that load, and the time lost each time the green changes (4 s per phase here), into a cycle length, and each phase gets green in proportion to its load. I add one check Webster does not make: a pedestrian crossing needs at least 7 s to start, plus the time to cross at 1.2 m/s, and a shorter green is lengthened.
The two phases run along the street grid’s north-south, then its east-west, with grid north at about 305° on the compass, as in the city’s counts. At J040 almost nothing arrives from the north, where Ottawa is the one street no car may arrive along, which confirms the orientation.



The estimated cycles, second by second. Grey: amber and all-red, the time lost when the green changes.


At J040, at 16h on 18 December 2024, the total load was 0.29 and Webster’s cycle came to 24 s. At J051 the load was 0.38 and the cycle 27 s. The traffic is far from filling these lights, and both cycles are much shorter than any city would use, so I use my lower limit of 60 s. The green is then set by pedestrians and by the split of loads: 26 s each way at J040, and 38 s north-south against 14 s east-west at J051. That is a finding about Griffintown’s streets, and a warning: at these volumes traffic leaves the timing open, so it becomes a design choice.
J181, on Robert-Bourassa, is skipped, because three of its four approaches lie beyond the network and Webster needs them all.

title: Movement counts and light timing
text:
The other 29 lights
I weighed four options. One plan for all lights would give a main street and a side street the same green. Borrowing the split of a counted light on the same streets would use real counts, but only two lights were counted. Timing the lights from space syntax was ruled out, because S9 compares movement with space syntax and would end up measuring its own input. I chose to share the green by road class, the city’s own street hierarchy, already in S1.
The city’s 2007 review of its arterial network (PDF) gives each class a daily traffic range: main arteries carry over 30,000 vehicles, collectors 1,000 to 15,000. Managing the flow is “prépondérante” on main arteries and “peu” on collectors (Ville de Montréal 2007). The United States standard agrees: “In general, the higher the traffic volume is, the higher the functional classification will be” (FHWA 2023, p. 26, PDF). Since Webster (1958) shares the green by how full each approach is, a busier street should get more of it.
The counts agree. At all five counted junctions where the two streets differ in class, the higher class carried more traffic over the day: William, a collector, 2.5 times as much as Guy at J040, and Wellington, a secondary arterial, 8.5 to 29 times as much as Ann, Murray, Young and Shannon. Four of the five are on Wellington, so the sample is small.
Road class does not match Webster at the two counted lights. At J040 it would give 21 and 31 s where Webster gives 26 and 26, because at the busiest hour each lane is about as full on both streets. At J051 it would give 26 and 26 s where Webster gives 38 and 14, because the classes are equal but de la Montagne is busier. So class tells which street gets more green over a day, and says nothing of how much at a given hour. The counted lights therefore keep Webster, and the share by class stays a cautious 60 %.
The rule: each street arriving at a light belongs to one of the two axes, and each axis takes the highest class among its streets, from main arterial (with highway) down through secondary arterial and collector to local. If both axes have the same class, the two phases share the 52 s of usable green equally. If not, the higher class gets 60 % and the lower 40 %. No phase is shorter than its pedestrians need, and where they need more, the cycle grows. Where cars arrive on one axis only, the other phase is for pedestrians.
Of the 31 lights, 2 follow Webster from counts, 17 have one street of higher class, 7 have equal classes, and 5 have cars on one axis only, mostly at the edge where the cross street lies beyond the network. In S8 these become the light plans, and the 60 % share and the 60 s cycle will be sliders in the Lab. The city’s pedestrian-signal file uses the same intersection numbers as its light file: 30 of the 31 lights have pedestrian signals, all but Seigneurs and William.

title: Movement counts and light timing
text:
Assumptions
Two numbers are mine alone. The 60 s lower limit on the cycle (with 120 s as the upper) is my guess for a city centre, and it sets every cycle here. The 60 % share is my own choice too, since the counts show which street is busier and say nothing of the amount. The other values (lane capacity, time lost per phase, walking speed and walk interval) follow Webster or common practice, because Montréal publishes neither its amber and all-red times nor its walking speed. The lane counts from OpenStreetMap cover 866 of 870 car ways, and I checked them at three junctions only.
The counts themselves cover a few days each, in winter or spring. They show those days; a typical year is beyond them.

title: About Situ
text:
Situ is the prototype for my PhD research-creation project. It asks whether the spatial culture and urban rhythm of Griffintown, Montréal, can be mediated and archived through a game-like 3D experience. I look at two eras: today, and the 1920s to 1940s. I work from the city’s open data and from observation, and I read both through urban theory. Game design carries the result to a player.
Nothing in Situ archives anything yet. So far there is a foundation: the street network with its rules and buildings, and the measures I will test it against.

title: About Situ
text:
The idea

Spatial culture
Hillier described a spatial culture as “a distinctive way of ordering space” (Hillier 1989, quoted in Griffiths & von Lünen 2016, p. xxiii). Griffiths and von Lünen see the field as the link between how a built place works and what it comes to mean to the people who live in it (2016, p. xxi). Adams (2024, introduction) wants spatial culture to be “qualified and documented”, which is close to what an archive needs.


Rhythm
A street layout holds no time. Space syntax, the method Hillier and Hanson started for measuring how a street network is arranged (What space syntax is), tends to strip social practice of its time (Griffiths & von Lünen 2016, p. xxiii). In Rhythmanalysis, Lefebvre finds rhythm wherever energy is spent in a particular place and time (2004, p. 15). His own example is a Paris junction seen from his window: on red the pedestrians cross, on green the cars rush (p. 28). The light cycles in S3 model that beat. He also holds that where there is rhythm there is measure (p. 8), so counts and timings belong in Situ. I add time on purpose: when places are open and when streets are busy.


Archiving
An archive keeps two things: the evidence records give of how their maker worked, and the information they hold about people and places (Schellenberg 1956, pp. 139 to 140). Situ keeps both. The city data says what Griffintown is. My decision files and tests record how I turned it into a model, the layer that the London Charter, a set of principles for visualising cultural heritage by computer, calls paradata (2009, principle 4.6). The Seville principles ask that a reconstruction show what is real and what is not (López-Menchero & Grande, principle 4), and that others can test it (principle 7). So every decision in my files carries a status, such as confirmed, assumed, likely or open.
Rhythm is the hard part. Taylor separates the archive of lasting things from the repertoire of embodied practice, like walking to work or lingering at a corner, which needs people to be present (2003, pp. 19 to 20). Situ cannot store a rhythm the way it stores a street. It can keep traces such as counts and timings, and offer a place where the rhythm can be performed again: the game. The Seville principles warn against showing “lifeless cities” (principle 5.3).


What Situ has and what it lacks
Lefebvre describes three moments of social space (1991, pp. 38 to 40). Each kind of source in Situ lines up with one of them, so I use them as a checklist, with every row open to revision.

NoteFour readings I make, and how I defend them





These are my own interpretations of the sources, each with the strongest objection I know and what would show me wrong.

Lefebvre’s triad as a checklist
Lefebvre warns that his three moments lose their force as an abstract model (1991, p. 40), and laying them over software comes close to that. So I use the table only to see what is missing; for now the lived row is empty. The rows also leak: the counts are observation, yet the city decided where to count. If the rows cannot be kept apart at all, the table should show the crossings.


Where layout and movement disagree
A gap between space syntax and observed movement points to something besides the layout, such as a shop or a rule. Griffiths and von Lünen ask research to spell out that kind of gap (2016, p. xxi). The 1993 paper on natural movement, the share of walking the layout alone produces, itself shows shops multiplying the layout’s effect (Hillier et al. 1993, p. 31). A difference may also be plain error, from a wrong network or too few counts, so it counts only after each system’s tests. The reading is wrong if the differences vanish once errors are fixed, or follow no pattern.


Schellenberg’s two values
Schellenberg drew his distinction between evidence and information from government records (1956, pp. 139 to 140, 148), and a research model is no government agency. I borrow only the distinction, which he says he defines “quite arbitrarily” (p. 139), and the London Charter already carries it into visualisation. The borrowing fails if the two layers cannot be kept apart, so my corrections live in their own file and the city’s files stay untouched.


The game as a place to perform rhythm again
Taylor’s repertoire and Lefebvre’s rhythm both need bodies present, and play is embodied action too. Against this, a player alone in a simulation receives no memory from Griffintown’s people, and the game itself is code and data, an archive object. Lefebvre adds that the rhythmanalyst is closer to the poet than to “the statistician, who counts things” (2004, p. 23).
I accept most of this. The game keeps traces and sets up a new performance, without holding the original repertoire, so interviews and focus groups are in the plan. If players’ movement bears no relation to the recorded rhythms, the game performs nothing of Griffintown.






Space syntax as one measuring stick
Space syntax describes the layout. I use it only to measure, and the simulated walkers never read it. At the end, S9 compares where they went with what space syntax predicts and with the city’s counts. Where they agree, the layout may explain the movement. Where they differ, something else is at work, and that difference is what the archive should keep.

title: The walking network

The city’s street file (Géobase) draws streets and leaves out most paths away from them, including the Lachine Canal path and the park paths in Griffintown. So a missing path does double harm: its own place is empty, and the streets around it look less connected than they are.

A path counts as a duplicate when most of its length runs within 10 m of a street. Joining follows the S1 rules: a path end joins the nearest junction or street, and a street dead end may join the middle of a path. The gap may be 15 m across the island, and 25 m in Griffintown and at places I have checked on a photo, because only there have I looked. title: The walking network
text:
Risks
Every added path is a claim about where people can walk, so I want each to carry its evidence, a dated photo, that anyone can dispute. A connector could join two things that are separate in reality, which is why the gaps are short and every connector is listed. A real link could also stay unjoined, and the 73 crossings are listed so I can check them one by one. Near Griffintown the risk is low: one unjoined crossing within 800 m, four within 2 km.
Bike paths stand in for footpaths, and a few may be unpleasant or closed to walking, so I took only separated paths and multi-use trails. The city maps park footpaths less well than bike paths, and I checked only Griffintown on photos, so values far from it are less certain.

title: The walking network

The driving network
The vehicle network starts from every city line and leaves out the lines cars may not use under the S1 road classes, plus one small group of streets no car can reach. The rest stay exactly as the city drew them, highways included. Segment analysis reads every line as two-way, though one-way streets keep their direction in the data. I ran PlanX on it on 10 October, at radii of 1200 and 2000 m. The Sample 4 vehicle values came from a network with pedestrian ways in it; now no segment closed to cars carries a vehicle value (S2).

The 37 segments without a vehicle value should have none. They are paths and connectors, or streets closed to cars, such as the Allées or the pedestrian ends of Murray and Smith. Before October, 31 of them carried one, because the older Sample 4 vehicle analysis included pedestrian ways.

title: S2 Scores
text:
What changed in October
On 10 October I reran both analyses on the rebuilt networks. Inside Griffintown the order of streets barely moved: the rank agreement (Spearman’s correlation, where 1.00 means no street moved) was 0.99 or 1.00 for every measure I compared.
Two changes are real, and both follow from my own decisions. Rue Brennan and Rue Ann gained walking choice (the east end of Brennan from 0.00 to 0.90, Ann from 0.37 to 0.93), because I assumed they connect to the paths beyond them. If a photo shows those streets really stop, I will reject those decisions and the values will fall back. Murray and Smith lost vehicle choice: the driving network leaves out their pedestrian ends, by the same road rule S1 uses, so cars can no longer pass through there.
Values from different networks are different measurements, so the older Sample 4 values stay for reference and are never mixed with these.

Maps
The maps show four of the 13 values S2 holds for every street: walking at 800 m, about a ten-minute walk, and driving at 2000 m, a short trip by car. The radii are my choice. 400 to 800 m is the usual low radius in space syntax studies (van Nes & Yamu 2021, p. 65), and Hillier, Yang and Turner (2012, p. 165) found 2000 m often significant in city work. Neither source ties 2000 m to cars, and neither radius comes from Griffintown’s data.

title: S2 Scores
text:
How S2 is built
The values come from PlanX, the QGIS tool I use for the analysis, run on the walking network and the driving network. Each S1 segment takes the values of the analysed lines lying under it, within 1 m. A segment that finds too little gets no value, never a zero, and a written reason.

Blueprint





flowchart TB
  IN1[/"S1 segments<br/>264 segments"/]:::data
  IN2[/"Walking values<br/>47,197 analysed lines"/]:::data
  IN3[/"Vehicle values<br/>47,730 analysed lines"/]:::data
  CFG[/"Settings<br/>a test point every metre, within 1 m<br/>cover 95 % or 50 %"/]:::rule

  IN1 --> R["READ<br/>segments and analysed lines"]:::step
  IN2 --> R
  IN3 --> R
  R --> G["SORT<br/>walking lines into a 20 m grid"]:::step
  G --> W["WALKING MATCH<br/>test points and the same-kind rule,<br/>cover and a mean by length"]:::step
  CFG --> W
  R --> V["VEHICLE MATCH<br/>may cars use it, then the same street"]:::step
  W --> S["STATUS<br/>matched, split,<br/>partial or missing"]:::step
  V --> S
  S --> O1[/"values for every segment"/]:::out
  S --> O2[/"trace of every line used"/]:::out
  O1 --> T["checks"]:::test
  O2 --> T
  T --> X["stress tests"]:::test
  X --> VZ["maps"]:::test
  VZ --> WB["data for the Lab"]:::test

  classDef data fill:none,stroke:#8a8a8a,color:#e6e6e6
  classDef rule fill:none,stroke:#8a8a8a,stroke-dasharray:4 3,color:#a6a6a6
  classDef step fill:none,stroke:#e6e6e6,color:#e6e6e6
  classDef out fill:none,stroke:#e6e6e6,stroke-width:2px,color:#ffffff
  classDef test fill:none,stroke:#fe83cc,color:#fe83cc








The problem
S1 and the walking network were built from the same city lines, and each cut them in its own places: S1 where a park path joins a street, the walking network wherever a bike path joins one. So an S1 segment and an analysed line are often the same street with different ends. Rue des Seigneurs is one S1 segment over two analysed pieces with different values. Matching by id alone would hide that. Matching by shape finds both.


The matching rule



A made-up segment and the analysed lines under it.


I place a test point every metre or so along each S1 segment. Each point looks for the closest analysed line within 1 m, but only among lines of the same kind: a city street looks only at pieces of the same street in the city’s records, and a path or connector only at its own kind.
The cover is the share of the segment’s length that found a line. The value is the mean of the lines found, each weighted by the metres it shares with the segment, so with one line it is that line’s value exactly. With 95 % cover or more, the segment counts as matched, or as split when its value comes from two lines. Between 50 and 95 % it keeps its value and is marked partial, so the gap stays visible. Below 50 % it gets no value and a written reason. Today no segment is partial.
The same-kind rule matters near junctions, where a test point at the end of a street also lies within 1 m of the crossing street. Without it, a street could take some of its neighbour’s values, a risk the stress tests measure.


Vehicle values
The driving network keeps the city’s lines uncut, so every S1 piece of a street simply takes the vehicle value of the same city street id. First S2 asks, by the same rule S1 uses, whether cars may use the street. Streets closed to cars and every added path or connector are marked as not roads, with a written reason. A street open to cars but missing from the analysis would be marked missing. Today there are none.

title: S2 Scores
text:
Tests

Checks
Each check asks a plain question of the result, and all of them pass. The Lab lists the latest run.







Question
Answer




Does every S1 segment have exactly one row?
Yes


Is a value present exactly when it should be, and is every missing value empty, with a reason?
Yes


Can every walking value be rebuilt from the trace of analysed lines behind it?
Yes


Is any value invented, or outside the values of its lines?
No


Do values come only from the same kind of line, and from the same street for city streets?
Yes


Do vehicle values equal the vehicle analysis for the same street?
Yes



A seventh check only reports coverage, the numbers given under Result.






TipThe trace check caught a real problem



On the first run the trace check failed. The trace rounded the shared metres to two decimals, too coarse to rebuild the values exactly, so I now store them to six.




Stress tests
The stress tests ask how easily the result could go wrong, by changing one thing on purpose and measuring what moves.
Two runs on the same input give identical results. Any matching distance from 5 cm to 10 m gives the same result, and test points every 25 cm or every 5 m move a value by about 0.01 at most. Shaking every S1 point by up to 0.3 m changes one segment, a 15 m connector at Brennan, which then takes part of its value from the next connector. At 0.8 m six segments change status, mostly paths and connectors along the canal, and no value moves by more than 0.08.
The test that matters most turns the same-kind rule off. With nothing shaken, no segment then takes values from another line. Shaken by 0.8 m, 142 segments do, and the worst, the short Smith link, moves by 0.24 as it takes values from the streets at both its ends.



As the S1 points are shaken further, segments without the same-kind rule start taking values from crossing streets. With the rule, almost nothing moves.


The match is exact today because S1 and the walking network share coordinates, so the matching distance has no effect. If the geometry drifted, for example after someone edits S1 in QGIS, the same-kind rule would keep S2 honest.
The rule test also found a fault upstream. Before a fix, Rue Smith picked up 21 m from a connector lying on top of it: the C06 link, which joined Smith to its own other end. I fixed the rule in S1 (C06), and after the new PlanX run no such segment remains.

I gather the signs Mapillary detected within 30 m of the junction (getting the signs). Each has two readings of where it faces: Mapillary’s own angle, which I tested on stop signs, and the photo, since a sign whose face I can read is turned towards the camera. A tool cuts the sign out of each panorama and puts every photo of one junction on one sheet, beside what the machine read. From the sheet I write down one decision per finding, with the evidence, and S3 applies it at its next build (how S3 is built).
I call a decision likely when both readings point to the same street and the photo shows a sign that fits. I leave it open when the readings disagree or the photo does not show which way the sign faces. A sign newer than every photo stays open too.

title: S3 checks with photos
text:
What the photos showed
The photos settled the last turn-sign contradiction and all four no-entry disagreements. Six no-entry signs are now explained by a photo, and the places to check fell from 27 to 21.

Wellington and Ann (J006)



J006. Each photo with what Mapillary read and the street that reading points to. Photos: Mapillary, CC BY-SA 4.0.


This was the last place where S3’s turn signs contradicted each other, and the photos show three streets, each with its own sign. The green “straight only” on the west corner, seen in May 2022 and December 2023, faces Wellington arriving from the west (P01, likely). S3 had given it to the short split piece of Wellington, which caused the contradiction. The “left or right only” under the viaduct faces Rue Ann from the north (P02, likely). Mapillary read the green sign as its opposite, “no straight through”, so the photo decides and the label alone never does.
One question stays open (P03). In 2024 a “straight only” sign stood under the viaduct, facing the short split piece of Wellington. In October 2025 the city installed a new post there with a stop and “left or right only”. No photo is newer, so S3 follows the city post and keeps the question on the list.


End of Brennan (J189)



J189. The end of Brennan in May 2024. Photos: Mapillary, CC BY-SA 4.0.


Bollards cross the street, and the no-entry signs at them close the paved area beyond to cars (P04, likely). The city file is right that cars may drive up to the bollards. The paving continues past them, which fits S1’s assumption C04 that walkers carry on, though it does not show where the paving leads, so C04 stays an assumption.


East end of Bassins (J122)



J122. The east end of Rue des Bassins. Photos: Mapillary, CC BY-SA 4.0.


The no-entry sign hangs under a stop sign, and Mapillary’s angle points within 2° of the path into the new park, closing the park to cars (P05, likely). Rue des Bassins itself stays two-way, as the city file says.


Notre-Dame and Inspecteur (J045)



J045. The corner of Notre-Dame and Inspecteur. Photos: Mapillary, CC BY-SA 4.0.


The two readings disagree, so the photo alone would leave it open. OpenStreetMap settles it: it draws Inspecteur north of Notre-Dame as two one-way halves, and the sign guards the half coming towards Notre-Dame (P07, likely). The city’s single two-way line is coarser, and fine for S1, which works at the scale of whole streets.


Still open



J146. The park path off Rue William. Photos: Mapillary, CC BY-SA 4.0.


At the park path off William (P06), the two readings are far apart, and the photos show the signs without showing which way they face. Two more no-entry signs, at the park connectors (J145), stand on recent posts that no photo shows. With P03 at Wellington and Ann, these remain open.

title: S3 checks with photos
text:
Limits
Most of the photos come from the city’s own survey car, taken from 2022 to 2024, so a sign installed after the last photo cannot be checked this way. Mapillary’s labels and angles are only a first guess: one label said the opposite of the sign, and at J045 the two readings disagreed. Each decision is mine and records how sure I am and why, so anyone can look at a sheet and disagree with it.
