title: How S4 is built and tested
text:
The sources







Source
What S4 takes from it




OpenStreetMap, with its building parts
building outlines and tags, including tower parts with their storeys; places such as shops and cafés, with opening hours


Ville de Montréal, tax roll (Unités d’évaluation foncière), also with lot outlines (October 2026)
each property’s use, storeys, dwellings, year built and floor area, and the land it sits on


Ville de Montréal, Adresse ponctuelle
where each street number stands


Ville de Montréal, Locaux commerciaux et statuts d’occupation
every ground-floor commercial space in 2025, occupied or vacant


Ville de Montréal, Lieux et bâtiments à vocation publique
public places and their opening hours


Situ S1
the streets people can walk on



The city’s files are open under CC BY 4.0, OpenStreetMap under ODbL.
The Concordia NGCI building file gives a height and a use for every building in Montréal. It carries no licence, though, so S4 does not use it, and I publish nothing made from it until one is granted; it also records a condo tower such as 2199 rue Ann, 76 m tall, as one dwelling. Québec City’s building file does not cover Montréal. The city’s 3D model of 2020 (Bâtiments 3D 2020) measures roofs but leaves out Le Sud-Ouest, Griffintown’s borough, holding only three small structures by Rue Notre-Dame at the edge of the study area (certain). Its 2016 model of Le Sud-Ouest predates most towers here, and I have not used it yet.
crumbs: How S4 is built and tested

title: How S4 is built and tested
text:
The outlines
Only OpenStreetMap draws buildings; every other source is a list of points or rows. So S4 starts from its outlines, keeping each one whose centre falls inside the study area. When the centre of one outline lies inside a larger one, S4 treats the smaller as a part of the larger, as with Griffix on Rue Wellington, a 21-storey tower drawn over a 2-storey base.
crumbs: How S4 is built and tested

title: How S4 is built and tested
section: The tax roll at its address
text:
The tax roll at its address
S4 matches each property’s street name and number to the city’s address points. Many rows found no match, because I downloaded the roll for whole streets across the island and the address points only around Griffintown. I once thought none of the missed rows stood in the study area; the lot outlines showed that 64 do, and they now count through their lot.
crumbs: How S4 is built and tested

title: How S4 is built and tested
text:
Every row finds its building
The city also publishes the roll with the outline of each property’s lot, the land it is taxed on, which every condo unit repeats. A lot is firmer ground than an address point, a single dot placed near a door or a curb, so S4 reads the lot first.
The buildings on a lot are those whose centre it holds or, failing that, any covering at least 30% of it. When the lot holds one building, the row goes there. When it holds several, the address point says which, and if the point stands in none of them, the nearest building within 15 m takes the row. When the lot holds no building, the address point works alone in the same way. Beyond 15 m a row stays unplaced, with the reason, since a longer reach risks the wrong building (stress tests).
Lot and point sometimes disagree. On a lot with one building, the lot decides. On a lot with several, where the point stands in a building off the lot, the point decides, since the lot cannot choose. Each such case becomes a checkpoint, ten so far.
Griffix is why the lot comes first. Its 197 flats, at 1045 rue Wellington, have their address point inside MaryRobert next door, where S4 used to count them, though their lot holds Griffix alone. Now they count in Griffix, and MaryRobert drops from 678 dwellings to 491.
crumbs: How S4 is built and tested

title: How S4 is built and tested
text:
The use
Each property’s land-use code begins with a digit naming a broad family, such as residential or commerce. A building takes the commonest family among its properties, leaving out condo parking spaces and storage units. A tie goes to the larger floor area, and a missing area is never read as zero. When the roll cannot decide, the OpenStreetMap tag speaks; a plain “building” tag names no use, so the use stays empty, with the reason. Every tie goes on my list to check, because it often means two buildings share one outline: at Ardent Mills, a 74-dwelling social housing property shares the flour mill’s.
crumbs: How S4 is built and tested

title: How S4 is built and tested
text:
Size
A building is as tall as its tallest known part. S4 takes the largest storey count from the roll or from OpenStreetMap, where every part inside the outline counts too, and notes its source. Condo units are left out, since the roll gives each only its own floor. I added the parts after an audit found MaryRobert at 2 storeys, its outline carrying only the podium; it now reads 22, from its tower. Where the dwellings cannot fit and no part helps, the building goes on my list to check. Its dwellings are the roll’s dwellings summed over its properties.
crumbs: How S4 is built and tested

title: How S4 is built and tested
text:
Ground floor and places
The premises are the 2025 survey’s spaces inside the building, vacant ones included. The places are anywhere a person might go: some from OpenStreetMap, the rest from the city’s public places and the survey’s occupied shops, leaving out benches and bike racks. A survey shop and an OpenStreetMap shop with exactly the same name in the same building become one place. A looser match, like Orangetheory Fitness against Orangetheory Theory, would be a guess, so S4 leaves it alone.

title: How S4 is built and tested
text:
The access link
S4 links each building to the nearest S1 street people can walk on, within 80 m, to stand in for the door. Every building’s record marks it as the weakest value in S4.

title: How S4 is built and tested
text:
Tests

The checks
Each check asks one plain question of the finished buildings.







Question
Answer




Does every outline appear once, as a building or as part of one?
Yes: 296 buildings, and one tower drawn over its podium


Does every value name its source, and every empty one its reason?
Yes


Can every count be rebuilt from the source files?
Yes


Is every property and shop in one building or listed as unplaced, never twice?
Yes


Does each use follow its rule, ties included?
Yes


Is every building linked to a walkable street within 80 m, or does it say why not?
Yes. Six links exceed 30 m; Hangar 1825 has none


Is every place in or next to its building, with each shop listed twice pointing to its twin?
Yes, with 52 such pairs


Is any building lower than its tallest known part?
No. Nine take their storeys from a tower part


Does every property sit where its lot or address point puts it, with a checkpoint when the two disagree?
Yes



One more check reports how much the sources cover; a gap there is a fact about the sources, never a failure. The Lab shows the latest results.


What the checks changed
The property check failed on its first run: 89 properties were counted twice, because the tax roll came in overlapping pages. S4 now keeps one row per property.
On the first map of uses, Ardent Mills, the flour mill, was painted residential. The roll puts a residential and an industrial property in its outline, and my first rule broke the tie by the order of a list, a choice I never made on purpose. Ties now follow the floor-area rule in the use.
The height check came from an audit: I set MaryRobert back to 2 storeys, and the check named it at once, since a part of it has 22. The same audit found an error in the arithmetic. Computed from map coordinates in the millions of metres, some outline centres lost their small digits and fell tens of metres off, enough to put four small outlines falsely inside their neighbours. S4 now measures each outline from its own first corner, and the false overlaps are gone.






TipTesting the tests



A test that always passes proves nothing. So I broke the finished buildings file four ways: I removed the reason from an unknown use, added one dwelling to a building, changed one use that came from the roll, and wrote 0 into an empty dwelling count. The checks caught all four. I did the same to the Lab’s copy of the results, which a further check compares with S4 down to every outline point: an unknown dwelling count turned to 0, one use changed, one point moved by 1 m, one place dropped. That check caught all four too.




Stress tests
Run twice on the same input, S4 gives the same output, line for line. The other stress tests ask how much the result depends on my choices.
The 15 m reach, within which a stray address point joins the nearest building, matters a lot at first and then very little. With no reach, 1,322 rows would be left out. At 15 m, 468 are, 415 of them at the one address point of checkpoint B01. At 30 m, two more find a building, and no property moves to another.
The last test shakes every address point by 2 m, then 5 m, as if the city had placed them a little off. At 2 m, 244 properties change building; at 5 m, 278. The total stays at 11,954 dwellings. An earlier run gave 625 at 5 m, partly because each point’s random move depended on the order the points were read in, so adding the lots reshuffled every move; each point now has its own fixed move. Without lots the test gives 291 at 5 m, so the lots barely change this number (certain): most properties sit on lots with several buildings, where the address point still decides.
That result is the warning. All the units at one address point move together, so where two buildings share a wall, a point a little off carries a whole condo tower into its neighbour. A single building’s count can be wrong while the block’s total is right. S5 and S7 should read dwellings by block, or with that in mind.

title: How S5 is built and tested
text:
From quarter-hours to hours
The city counts in 15-minute slices, by kind of road user. S5 keeps every slice counted within 15 m of an S1 junction, the same rule as the counts page, and sums it by mode, keeping people on foot and bicycles apart from motor vehicles of every kind. A slice with nobody in it stays a counted zero, which differs from a slice nobody counted.
An hour gets a value only when all four of its quarters were counted. Several of the one-day windows open or close on the half hour, so their edge hours are partial: 16 hours at the junctions, 48 rows across the modes, stay empty, each with the number of quarters it had. S5 never stretches a part of an hour into a whole one.
crumbs: How S5 is built and tested

title: How S5 is built and tested
text:
The day’s shape
A busy junction and a quiet one can share a rhythm, so S5 compares each day with itself. The reference hours are the hours counted in full on every day: 7h, 8h, 11h, 12h, 16h and 17h. Each day, for each mode, is divided by its own mean over those six hours, so 1.0 is an ordinary daytime hour of that day. Two of the six fall in each of the city’s windows, so no window outweighs another.
A weekday hour takes the mean of every day that counted it, and keeps their lowest and highest values. Each value names the days behind it, so it can be rebuilt by hand. Outside the reference hours, most hours rest on J040 alone, and S5 marks them.
Only Tuesdays, Wednesdays and Thursdays were counted. S5 lets their shape stand in for Monday and Friday, and says so on every such row. Saturday and Sunday stay empty, with the reason.
crumbs: How S5 is built and tested

title: How S5 is built and tested
text:
Bicycle detectors
The city’s permanent bicycle detectors report every hour, by site, direction and lane. S5 keeps the detectors whose point lies inside the study area, by the same test S4 uses for buildings: Peel at Ottawa, northbound and southbound, and William at Nazareth, westbound. Two detectors on Peel at Notre-Dame stand 35 and 49 m from junction J187, outside the area, and S5 lists them without using them.
A recorded hour of 0 stays 0, and a missing hour is a gap. A detector’s day counts only when all 24 hours were recorded, and the Griffintown day sums the three detectors on days when every one is complete: 376 days. Each such day is divided by its own mean over the same reference hours as the counts, then grouped by kind of day (weekday, Saturday, Sunday) and season. A group keeps its mean and its middle half, the range of the central half of its days.
The seasons are the meteorological ones: winter from December to February, spring from March to May, and so on. Holidays are not set apart, so a public holiday on a Monday counts as a weekday.

title: How S5 is built and tested
text:
Reading opening hours
OpenStreetMap writes hours in a small grammar, like Mo-Fr 07:00-22:00; Sa 08:00-20:00; Su off. S5 reads the part of it Griffintown’s places use. Rules separated by a semicolon replace what earlier rules said about the same days; a rule after a comma adds to them. A day the text never names is closed, which is the tag’s own convention. Hours that run past midnight carry into the next morning, so a bar open 17:00-03:00 on Saturday is open early on Sunday. An opening with no closing time, a note such as “sur rdv” (by appointment), or a text S5 cannot parse leaves those hours unknown. Public holidays are set aside, since S5 has no calendar yet.
The city’s list of public places writes its hours in French, day by day, and sometimes for a season only: the play fountains at Place des Aiguilleurs open from 21 May and close from 22 September. S5 keeps the season with the place.
A place counts as open in an hour when it is open at half past. A place with no hours is unknown at every hour, never closed.

title: How S5 is built and tested
text:
Tests

Twelve checks
Each check asks one plain question of what S5 wrote. Ten must pass, and all ten do; the last two only report. The Lab shows the latest results.









Question
Answer




T1
Does the evidence hold every counted quarter-hour, with the same totals as the city’s file?
yes, 1,440 quarters


T2
Does an hour get a value only when all four quarters were counted?
yes; 48 partial hours stay empty


T3
Were the reference hours counted every day, and does each day average 1 over them?
yes


T4
Can every hour of the weekday shape be rebuilt from the days it names?
yes


T5
Do Saturday and Sunday stay empty, with the reason?
yes


T6
Is every S4 place here once, and is a place without readable hours unknown at every hour?
yes, 610 places


T7
Does the hours reader give the expected week on fixed examples?
yes, 16 examples


T8
Does every place’s week come from its own hours text, and do the counts per hour add up?
yes


T9
Do the detector days hold every recorded hour, with a total only when all 24 were recorded?
yes; 309 incomplete detector-days left without a total


T10
Can every bicycle shape and monthly level be rebuilt from the detector hours?
yes, 376 days


T11
How much do the sources cover?
report: 17 of 24 weekday hours rest on J040 alone; 83 of 558 places give hours


T12
Do the counts and the detectors agree on a weekday’s bicycles?
report: correlation 0.87 in winter, 0.89 over all seasons









TipTesting the tests



A test that always passes proves nothing. So I broke the finished files five ways: I gave Saturday at 8h a value, turned one unknown hour of a place without hours into closed, added one person to one counted hour, filled a partial hour, and changed one letter of a place’s week in the Lab’s copy. Each was caught: the first by T4 and T5, the second by T6 and T8, the third by T1 and T4, the fourth by T1 and T2, and the last by the Lab’s check L7. Then I put the files back.




Stress tests
Run twice on the same input, S5 gives the same output (X1). The other stress tests ask how much the shape depends on so few days.
X2 leaves out one counted day at a time. In the reference hours, which nine days share, no value moves by more than 0.12, and for people on foot and cars by no more than 0.06. In the hours J040 holds alone, the three December days disagree more: leaving out one of them moves people on foot by up to 0.12 and bicycles by up to 0.44, since a few cyclists in an hour make a large share. The bicycle values at night and in mid-afternoon are the weakest numbers in S5.
X3 leaves out one junction at a time. The busiest hour stays 17h for every mode, with one exception: without J040, the bicycles’ busiest hour moves to 8h. So the evening cycling peak leans on J040.
X5 leaves out one month of detector days at a time. Weekday shapes hold well, moving by at most 0.05 in summer and 0.04 in autumn. Weekend shapes rest on fewer days and move more, up to 0.46 for a winter Sunday, and spring is the thinnest season, with 22 weekdays, 8 Saturdays and 9 Sundays.
X4 changes what “open in this hour” means. Of the other readings I tried, the strictest, open for the whole hour, removes 75 of the week’s 5,626 open place-hours, and the others move fewer. The choice of half past hardly matters.

title: How S6 is built and tested
section: Values as the source gives them
text:
Values as the source gives them
S6 copies each value and changes none. A tree with no planting date keeps an empty date and the reason. A hydrant whose installation date is the city’s placeholder, 1 January 1900, keeps no date. A bench whose OpenStreetMap entry has no tags keeps none.
crumbs: How S6 is built and tested

title: How S6 is built and tested
text:
Objects found in photos
Mapillary’s software may place the same object twice, or see the two heads of one pole as two lights. S6 joins detections of one kind that lie within 3 m of each other, in a chain, and places the object at their mean. Each object keeps every detection it holds, the date of the first photo that shows it and the date of the last. Zebra stripes and plain crosswalk lines are both a crossing.
An object found by Mapillary’s software and one of the same kind in OpenStreetMap less than 5 m apart are taken to be the same object, and each names the other. An object the software has found in no photo since 2023 becomes a checkpoint.

title: How S6 is built and tested
section: The street each object stands on
text:
The street each object stands on
Each object belongs to the nearest S1 segment within 30 m. An object farther away keeps no street and says why: most are trees in parks, or benches and tables along the canal path. The stress test below shows that the distance only decides whether an object has a street, never which one.
crumbs: How S6 is built and tested

title: How S6 is built and tested
text:
Width of a sidewalk
The city draws sidewalks as outlines and gives no width. S6 estimates a mean width as twice the area divided by the perimeter, which is exact for a long thin strip and a little low for short pieces. The median piece comes out about 2.3 m wide. A piece wider than 10 m on average would be listed for a look, since it is more likely a plaza or a joined drawing; none is.

Signs: what they mean
The Québec standard for road signs, Tome V, Signalisation routière, is sold and was out of my reach, so I used free sources. The Règlement sur la signalisation routière on LégisQuébec, current to 1 June 2026, gives the legal meaning of each kind of sign. The ministry’s 2026 posters (Québec.ca) and its online catalogue, the Répertoire des dispositifs, give their names and pictures.

The code numbers differ between sources: the regulation numbers the turn bans P-110-6 to P-110-8, while the 2026 poster shows P-110-62 for “no left turn”. So S3 reads a sign’s written meaning and ignores its code.
None of these sources says where a sign stands, before or after the junction. The only text on placement I found is a 2001 provincial guide quoting Tome V: turn signs stand “à proximité de l’endroit où la manœuvre doit être effectuée”, near where the turn is made (BAnQ). That does not say which corner, so placement has to be read from photos, one junction at a time.

title: Checking the sources
section: PlanX: how far is a radius?
text:
PlanX: how far is a radius?
PlanX is the QGIS tool that gives each street segment its space syntax values, such as choice (roughly how often a street lies on the way between other places) and integration (roughly how easy it is to reach), each measured within a radius (what these are). Its manual (version 4.18, September 2026) calls the radius “metric radii in map units”, without saying whether 800 m runs along the streets or in a straight line, two very different neighbourhoods.
PlanX reports how many other segments each one found within the radius. For twelve Griffintown segments I counted again in two ways: the segments I can walk to within the radius, and those whose middle lies inside a circle of that radius. At 800 m, PlanX’s counts came to 0.89 of the walking counts and 0.57 of the circle counts; at 400 m, 0.92 and 0.53.
So the radius is measured along the streets (certain), and S2 reads it that way. PlanX’s counts sit a little under mine, most likely because it measures metres along the path with the fewest turns, which is a bit longer than the shortest (likely). I could not reproduce the counts exactly, so that detail stays open.
The manual also says the network has no direction, so the vehicle values describe the street layout without its one-way rules. I checked its normalised forms of choice and integration (NACH and NAIN, which can be compared between networks of different sizes) against the published papers in Reading closely. NACH matches Hillier, Yang and Turner (2012, p. 191) exactly, and PlanX counts each pair of segments once, the same definition as Turner (2007, p. 544) (how I found out). For NAIN the paper gives two other forms, which put the streets in the same order; the numbers compare only within one form.

title: Checking the sources
section: Mapillary: which way does a sign face?
text:
Mapillary: which way does a sign face?
Mapillary reads its street photos with a machine and maps every sign it sees, with a compass angle. If that angle is the way the sign faces, it can settle which street a sign controls.

Getting the signs
I asked Mapillary for every feature it has mapped around the S1 network, in squares of about 400 m because it refuses large ones, and kept the traffic signs unchanged, with their dates. On 10 October that gave 1,455 signs, 838 of them regulatory, among them 235 stop detections and 88 no-entry signs.


Testing the direction on signs we already know
A stop sign faces the drivers it stops, and S3 already knows, for every city stop post, which street those drivers arrive along. So the right answer is known in advance. For each city stop post I took the nearest Mapillary stop sign within 15 m and compared.



Left: the idea. Right: the test. Pink bars are posts where Mapillary’s angle is within 45° of facing the drivers.


Of 139 city stop posts, 99 had a Mapillary stop sign within 15 m. For 69 of those, the angle was within 45° of facing the drivers, and only one pointed the way they travel. The median difference was 21°.
So the angle is the way the sign faces (likely). A smaller group sits near 90° off, with a simple cause (likely): at an all-way stop, four stop signs stand within a few metres, and the nearest one can face the cross street. The main peak sits about 15° off zero, and I do not know why yet. Fifteen degrees never confuses two streets meeting at a junction, so it does not change how I use the angle. Still, a machine reading is evidence to check. Where a sign’s placement was in doubt, S3 uses Mapillary’s facing and then the photo itself (S3 checks with photos).
